newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Spieker sees Q2 FFO above estimates.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Spieker sees Q2 FFO above estimates.

text.p: Spieker Properties Inc said Friday it expects funds from operations for the second quarter to be slightly above the First Call mean estimate of $0.61 a share.

"I think we'll modestly exceed that expectation," Craig Vought, chief financial officer of the Menlo Park, California-based real estate investment trust, said in an interview. He said the company, which owns and operates office and industrial properties in California and the Pacific Northwest, should exceed the First Call estimate by "a couple pennies, but not three."

Among the things driving growth in funds from operations, an accepted measure of a real estate investment trust's overall performance, are the increases in rents the company gets when old leases expire, or the rollover rate.

"We will announce on Tuesday, rollover numbers ... at twice the growth rates we've seen in the past," Vought said, referring to the scheduled release of the company's second quarter financial report. Spieker has previously been able to implement rent increases of 10-15 percent.

"It won't be like that every quarter, there's no question about that," Vought said. "But we're entering a period where most, but not all of the leases in the company that are rolling over are going to be rolling at higher levels."
The markets the company operates in have benefitted from the stronger California economy and strong technology sector.
At the same time, there is very little new construction in Spieker's markets, Vought said.

Spieker itself is trying to pick up its pace of new property development, Vought said. The company had about $145 million in its development pipeline at the end of the first quarter and could add another $100 million by the end of the year, Vought said.

"What we really look for is good sites, close to tranportation, close to services and close to where we think people want to live," he said. Unlike some developers that "build to suit" specific large tenants' needs, Spieker does not build to suit and focuses on attracting smaller tenants that demand less in the way of capital improvements, he said.
Spieker has also had a healthy pace of acquisitions, with a little over $625 million spent on new property so far this year.
That pace is unlikely to continue if Spieker continues to purchase single properties at a time, Vought said.

But the company is currently looking at property portfolios on the market and if it purchased one of those portfolios, its acquisition spending could be similar to the first half of the year, he said.
Spieker shares were up 1/8 at 38-1/4 Friday.
